methods.label: Construct a square in the plane of ABC
methods.explanation:
The parallel-plane condition lets us copy the direction of \(DE\) into the plane of \(ABC\). We will use this to construct a square whose diagonal is \(AC\).

First, the right triangle \(ABC\) gives
\[
AC^2=AB^2+BC^2=4+4=8.
\]
Let \(\Pi\) be its plane. Using the given right angles at \(E\) and \(D\), complete rectangles \(EDFA\) and \(EDCG\), with vertices in the stated cyclic orders. Thus
\[
AF\parallel GC\parallel DE,\qquad AF=GC=2,
\]
and
\[
DF=EA=2,\qquad EG=DC=2.
\]
Because \(DE\parallel\Pi\), the lines through \(A\) and \(C\) parallel to \(DE\) lie in \(\Pi\). Hence \(F\) and \(G\) both lie in \(\Pi\).

The equal, parallel opposite sides \(AF\) and \(GC\) make \(AFCG\) a parallelogram. Also, both \(DF\) and \(DC\) are perpendicular to \(DE\) at \(D\). Therefore \(F\) and \(C\) lie in the plane through \(D\) perpendicular to \(DE\), so \(FC\perp AF\). The parallelogram is consequently a rectangle. Applying Pythagoras to \(AFC\) gives
\[
FC^2=AC^2-AF^2=8-4=4.
\]
Thus \(AFCG\) is a square of side \(2\).

Within \(\Pi\), a point at distance \(2\) from both \(A\) and \(C\) has only two possible positions. It lies on the perpendicular bisector of \(AC\), and Pythagoras fixes its distance from the midpoint of \(AC\), leaving one point on each side of \(AC\). The square shows that these two points are \(F\) and \(G\). Since \(AB=BC=2\), we must have \(B=F\) or \(B=G\).

If \(B=F\), its perpendicular distance from \(DE\) is \(DF=2\). If \(B=G\), that distance is \(EG=2\). Both possibilities therefore give
\[
[BDE]=\frac12\cdot DE\cdot2
=\frac12\cdot2\cdot2=2,
\]
choice \(\mathrm{C}\).
